items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: So we asked Sid Catlett to play with us until Mary Lou arrived. That was a unique replacement for a piano, but with Sid on drums, and Al Hall being the solid bass player that he was, the piano was hardly missed

ctx.x: I gigged and did many Sunday afternoon jam sessions at Jimmy Ryan's and few in Boston at the Ken Club. Once in Boston I jammed with Pete Brown and another time with Coleman Hawkins. The sessions at Jimmy Ryan's which was across the street from the Famous Door and the three Dances on 52nd Street, were presented by Milt Gabler who owned the Commodore Record Shop near the Grand Central station on East 42nd Street.

Jack Crystal who worked in Milt's record shop was in charge of the session which featured many well known black and white musicians: Art Hodes, Pee Wee Russell, Bobby Hackett, George Wettling, Rod Cless, Sid Catlett, Hank Duncan, Sandy Williams, Wild Bill Davison and Oran "Hot Lips" Page to name a few that participated in these sessions which really jumped. There were always two bottles of whisky furnished by Milt to get the sessions in a swinging mood. The closing number was always 'Bugle Call Rag' and I'm…

One day, Al Hall came to my house and asked me if I would like to replace a guitarist named Billy Moore who was sick in a hospital. My brother(who was a tailor) and I were sharing a three-roomed furnished apartment on 161st Street and I had not seen Al for quite some time. He told me that he was working at the Cafe Society Uptown with Billy Moore and a pianist.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Sammy Stewart was another orchestra from Chicago that came to the Savoy when I was there... On drums was Big Sid Catlett.

ctx.x: The first time I played with three trumpets was when Gus Mo Clung, whom I had first heard with Scott, came back in the orchestra. Gus had a dispute with Don Redman when Scott had been in New York long before I joined them. Gus played with Clarence Page in Cincinnati in preparation to joining the Cotton Pickers after he left Scott and when Don was engaged to lead the Cotton Pickers, the first thing he did was to fire Gus.

So Gus joined our band in Cincinnati and Lloyd let Frank Newton go when we returned to the Savoy. We were in the Savoy when Marion Hardy's Alabamians came with Cab Calloway who sang through a megaphone three feet long. Eddie Mallory, one of the trumpet players became one of the ex-husbands and Charlie 'Fat Man' Turner eventually opened a bar called 'Fat Man's' on 155th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue that became very popular. Cab took over the leadership of a band called the Missourians which eventually became his…

Fletcher Henderson was engaged for one night and we had played some numbers which I don't remember what it was, but the dancers did not want us to stop and we played for a half hour longer before we finally left the stand and when the public saw that we were not coming back,
